title: Applying فِعْل الْأَمْر Across the Qur'ān, Its Two Exceptions, and Lesson 15: النَّهْي
summary: The tamrīnāt of lesson fourteen are worked through on page 96, deriving the command for verb after verb and sorting them into the three groups set by the vowel on the third letter. The teacher traces nearly every one to a Qur'ānic command — from the wuḍū' āyah to Nūḥ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام telling his son ارْكَبْ مَعَنَا — flags كُلْ and خُذْ as the only two exceptions so far, and then introduces النَّهْي, the prohibition, which is simply لَا with the مُضَارِع made sākin at the end.
key_points: The commands sort into three groups by the vowel on the third letter of the مُضَارِع: ḍamma gives اُقْتُلْ، اُكْتُبْ، اُدْخُلْ; kasra gives اِجْلِسْ، اِغْسِلْ، اِنْزِلْ; fatḥa gives اِفْتَحْ، اِذْهَبْ، اِحْفَظْ، اِلْعَبْ، اِرْكَبْ، اِقْرَأْ.
Two sākin letters cannot meet, so when a word beginning with one follows a command the command's final sukūn becomes a kasra: اُكْتُبْ plus الدَّرْسَ is read اُكْتُبِ الدَّرْسَ.
هَمْزَة الْوَصْل is not pronounced when the command falls inside the sentence — يَا حَامِدُ اكْتُبْ — which conveniently removes the need to work out whether the hamza would carry a ḍamma or a kasra.

Only two exceptions to the rule have come up: كُلْ from أَكَلَ، يَأْكُلُ and خُذْ from أَخَذَ، يَأْخُذُ. In both, the two hamzas the rule would produce are dropped because they are awkward to pronounce. Their plurals are كُلُوا and خُذُوا.
النَّهْي (al-nahy : prohibition) is the opposite of الْأَمْر and is formed simply: اِفْعَلْ becomes لَا تَفْعَلْ, اِذْهَبْ becomes لَا تَذْهَبْ.
The sukūn at the end is what makes it a prohibition. لَا تَخْرُجْ is don't go out, a command; لَا تَخْرُجُ with a ḍamma is a statement — you are not going out. The jazm is the whole difference.
فَهِمَ، يَفْهَمُ gives اِفْهَمْ, used much as a teacher would say pay attention — أَقُولُ لَكَ هَذَا وَأُؤَكِّدُ هَذَا فَافْهَمْ.
عَلِمَ gives اِعْلَمْ, and in فَاعْلَمْ the hamza is not pronounced because of the preceding فَـ.
سَكَنَ means to live somewhere and needs no preposition: اُسْكُنْ الْجَنَّةَ already means live in Paradise, whereas other verbs would require فِي.
غَرِيب in Arabic means a stranger, someone not from the area — not poor, as the similar word means in Urdu.

Vocabulary from the drills: سَيْف (sword), حِذَاء (shoe), دَرَّاجَة (bicycle), عَصَا (staff), قَرْيَة (village), مَقْعَد (seat), مَجَلَّة (magazine), حَقِيبَة (bag), أَجْوِبَة as the plural of جَوَاب, إِنَّمَا (only), and يَكَادُ (to be about to).
Verbs introduced: طَبَخَ (to cook), حَلَقَ، يَحْلِقُ (to shave), كَسَرَ، يَكْسِرُ (to break), قَطَعَ (to cut), مَنَعَ (to prevent), ضَحِكَ (to laugh), and رَنَّ، يَرِنُّ (to ring).
A milestone the teacher drew attention to: اقْرَأْ بِاسْمِ رَبِّكَ الَّذِي خَلَقَ, the first āyah ever revealed, can now be understood word for word with nothing in it the class has not covered.
questions: [00:01:00] Q: Why does that word take a kasra — is there a حَرْف الجَرّ behind it? — A: No; two sākin letters cannot be pronounced together, so the first takes a kasra instead.
[00:09:00] Q: What does مِنْ do to the following word? — A: It gives it a kasra, as a حَرْف الجَرّ.
[00:13:00] Q: Does the حَرْف الجَرّ affect the كَ at the end? — A: No, because the كَ is a pronoun, and pronouns do not change.
[00:14:00] Q: Why is it كُلْ rather than the form the rule would give? — A: Because the rule would produce two hamzas, which are hard to pronounce, so they were dropped — the same as with خُذْ.
[00:25:00] Q: What is the word for to destroy? — A: أَهْلَكَ، يُهْلِكُ, which is distinct from حَلَقَ، يَحْلِقُ, to shave.
[00:30:00] Q: Who said افْعَلْ مَا تُؤْمَرُ? — A: Ismāʿīl عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام, answering his father Ibrāhīm عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام about the dream.
[00:35:00] Q: What is the small mark written above the هَمْزَة الْوَصْل? — A: Just a symbol showing it is not to be pronounced; you need not write it yourself.
[00:40:00] Q: Where is the in of in Paradise in اسْكُنْ الْجَنَّةَ? — A: It is built into the verb. سَكَنَ does not need فِي, though other verbs would.
[00:43:00] Q: What is the difference between لَا تَخْرُجْ and لَا تَخْرُجُ? — A: The first, with the sukūn, is a prohibition — don't go out. The second is a statement that you are not going out.

quiz.q: Why is اُكْتُبْ الدَّرْسَ read as اُكْتُبِ الدَّرْسَ?
options: Because two sākin letters cannot meet, so the first takes a kasra
Because a حَرْف الجَرّ precedes it
Because the object requires a kasra
quiz.a: The rule against two successive sukūns turns the command's final sukūn into a kasra.

quiz.q: What happens to هَمْزَة الْوَصْل when the command appears mid-sentence, as in يَا حَامِدُ اكْتُبْ?
quiz.a: It is skipped in pronunciation, which also removes the need to decide between a ḍamma and a kasra on it.

quiz.q: Which two commands are the exceptions to the four-step rule?
quiz.a: From أَكَلَ and أَخَذَ, both would yield two hamzas, so the forms were shortened to كُلْ and خُذْ.

options: لَا with the مُضَارِع, its last letter made sākin
By adding a hamza to the command
quiz.a: اِذْهَبْ becomes لَا تَذْهَبْ — the simple inverse of the command.

quiz.q: What distinguishes لَا تَخْرُجْ from لَا تَخْرُجُ?
options: The sukūn makes the first a prohibition; the second is a statement
quiz.a: The jazm is the whole difference: don't go out, against you are not going out.

quiz.q: What is the command form of نَزَلَ، يَنْزِلُ?
quiz.a: The kasra on the third letter gives a kasra on the hamza: اِنْزِلْ, as in اِنْزِلْ مِنْ سَيَّارَتِكَ.

quiz.q: What is the command form of رَكِبَ، يَرْكَبُ?
quiz.a: A fatḥa on the third letter gives a kasra on the hamza — اِرْكَبْ, the form in يَا بُنَيَّ ارْكَبْ مَعَنَا.

quiz.q: What does غَرِيب mean in Arabic?
quiz.a: The teacher corrected the Urdu-influenced reading: in Arabic it means someone not from the area, a stranger.

quiz.q: Why does اسْكُنْ الْجَنَّةَ need no فِي?
options: Because سَكَنَ carries the sense of living in something without a preposition
Because the فِي is dropped in commands
quiz.a: Some verbs require a حَرْف الجَرّ to complete their meaning and some do not; سَكَنَ is one that does not.
Given as new vocabulary — إِنَّمَا أَنَا بَشَرٌ مِثْلُكُمْ, I am only a man like you.

quran_examples.arabic: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا قُمْتُمْ إِلَى الصَّلَاةِ فَاغْسِلُوا وُجُوهَكُمْ وَأَيْدِيَكُمْ إِلَى الْمَرَافِقِ وَامْسَحُوا بِرُءُوسِكُمْ وَأَرْجُلَكُمْ إِلَى الْكَعْبَيْنِ
quran_examples.transliteration: yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū idhā qumtum ilā al-ṣalāti fa-ghsilū wujūhakum wa-aydiyakum ilā al-marāfiqi wa-msaḥū bi-ruʾūsikum wa-arjulakum ilā al-kaʿbayn
quran_examples.translation: O you who have believed, when you rise to pray, wash your faces and your forearms to the elbows, and wipe over your heads and wash your feet to the ankles.
quran_examples.note: The teacher's example while correcting اِغْسِلْ: the wuḍū' āyah is built from plural commands, فَاغْسِلُوا and وَامْسَحُوا, whose hamzas go unpronounced after the preceding letters.

quran_examples.translation: Enter it in peace. This is the Day of Eternity.
quran_examples.note: Offered for اُدْخُلْ in the plural, with the teacher's hope that the class would one day hear it said to them.

quran_examples.arabic: فَقُلْنَا اضْرِب بِّعَصَاكَ الْحَجَرَ ۖ فَانفَجَرَتْ مِنْهُ اثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ عَيْنًا
quran_examples.transliteration: fa-qulnā ḍrib bi-ʿaṣāka al-ḥajar, fa-nfajarat minhu thnatā ʿashrata ʿaynā
quran_examples.translation: So We said: Strike the stone with your staff. And there gushed forth from it twelve springs.
quran_examples.note: A student's answer for اِضْرِبْ, spoken to Mūsā عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام; عَصَا (staff) was glossed here, and the āyah also carries the اثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ number form from an earlier lesson.

quran_examples.arabic: يَا بُنَيَّ ارْكَب مَّعَنَا وَلَا تَكُن مَّعَ الْكَافِرِينَ
quran_examples.transliteration: yā bunayya rkab maʿanā wa-lā takun maʿa al-kāfirīn
quran_examples.translation: O my son, come aboard with us and be not with the disbelievers.
quran_examples.note: A student's answer for اِرْكَبْ, spoken by Nūḥ عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام to his son — and the second half, وَلَا تَكُنْ, is itself a نَهْي of exactly the shape introduced later in the session.

quran_examples.arabic: كُلُوا وَاشْرَبُوا هَنِيئًا بِمَا أَسْلَفْتُمْ فِي الْأَيَّامِ الْخَالِيَةِ
quran_examples.transliteration: kulū wa-shrabū hanīʾan bi-mā aslaftum fī al-ayyāmi al-khāliyah
quran_examples.translation: Eat and drink in satisfaction for what you put forth in the days past.
quran_examples.note: Cited for the irregular كُلْ in its plural form كُلُوا, alongside the regular اشْرَبُوا.

quran_examples.arabic: يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا ارْكَعُوا وَاسْجُدُوا وَاعْبُدُوا رَبَّكُمْ وَافْعَلُوا الْخَيْرَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ
quran_examples.transliteration: yā ayyuhā alladhīna āmanū rkaʿū wa-sjudū wa-ʿbudū rabbakum wa-fʿalū al-khayra laʿallakum tufliḥūn
quran_examples.translation: O you who have believed, bow and prostrate and worship your Lord and do good, that you may succeed.
quran_examples.note: The āyah the teacher singled out as carrying four commands at once, noting that the sajdah verses commonly contain a form of اُسْجُدْ.

quran_examples.arabic: فَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ لَا إِلَٰهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
quran_examples.transliteration: fa-ʿlam annahu lā ilāha illā llāh
quran_examples.translation: So know that there is no deity except Allah.
quran_examples.note: Given for اِعْلَمْ, with the hamza unpronounced after the فَـ; it also shows أَنَّ following a verb, per the earlier rule.

quran_examples.arabic: وَاسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ الَّتِي كُنَّا فِيهَا وَالْعِيرَ الَّتِي أَقْبَلْنَا فِيهَا
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-sʾali al-qaryata allatī kunnā fīhā wa-l-ʿīra allatī aqbalnā fīhā
quran_examples.translation: And ask the city in which we were and the caravan in which we came.
quran_examples.note: Quoted for اِسْأَلْ, with the teacher recounting the brothers of Yūsuf pleading their case to Yaʿqūb عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام; قَرْيَة means village, standing here for its people.

quran_examples.arabic: قَالَ يَا أَبَتِ افْعَلْ مَا تُؤْمَرُ ۖ سَتَجِدُنِي إِن شَاءَ اللَّهُ مِنَ الصَّابِرِينَ
quran_examples.transliteration: qāla yā abati fʿal mā tuʾmaru, satajidunī in shāʾa llāhu mina al-ṣābirīn
quran_examples.translation: He said: O my father, do as you are commanded. You will find me, if Allah wills, among the steadfast.
quran_examples.note: Ismāʿīl عَلَيْهِ السَّلَام's reply to his father, given for اِفْعَلْ; يَا أَبَتِ also shows a مُضَاف after يَا.

quran_examples.arabic: وَيَا آدَمُ اسْكُنْ أَنتَ وَزَوْجُكَ الْجَنَّةَ
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-yā ādamu skun anta wa-zawjuka al-jannah
quran_examples.translation: And O Ādam, dwell, you and your wife, in Paradise.
quran_examples.note: The example behind the question about the missing فِي: سَكَنَ takes الْجَنَّةَ directly, with no preposition needed.

quran_examples.arabic: وَلَا تَحْلِقُوا رُءُوسَكُمْ حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ الْهَدْيُ مَحِلَّهُ
quran_examples.transliteration: wa-lā taḥliqū ruʾūsakum ḥattā yablugha al-hadyu maḥillah
quran_examples.translation: And do not shave your heads until the sacrificial animal reaches its place of slaughter.
quran_examples.note: Raised when حَلَقَ، يَحْلِقُ came up, and it is a نَهْي in the plural — لَا with the مُضَارِع — anticipating lesson fifteen.
